content: Koplik's spots are small, irregularly shaped red lesions that contain a tiny bluish-white center. These spots are typically observed on the buccal mucosa (the inner lining of the cheeks) and the lingual mucosa (the mucous membrane of the tongue). They are considered pathognomonic, meaning they are a definitive diagnostic sign, for the early stages of measles infection. These spots are named after Henry Koplik, an American pediatrician who first provided a detailed description of them in 1896. Koplik's spots usually appear a few days prior to the onset of the characteristic measles rash, making them a valuable early clinical indicator, particularly in children who have been exposed to the measles virus. Although Henry Koplik is credited with their detailed description, earlier observations of similar phenomena were made by other physicians. Some sources attribute the first description to Reubold in Würzburg in 1854, while others credit Johann Andreas Murray in the 18th century. Additionally, German internist Carl Jakob Adolf Christian Gerhardt noted similar findings in 1874, Danish physician N. Flindt in 1879, and Russian physician Nicolai Feodorowitsch von Filatov in 1897.
